chapter.name: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation

questions.q:
A university team has Rs 12 lakh. One more season of excavation at a site with only stone tools and animal fossils costs Rs 7.5 lakh. A decipherment project for a set of seal inscriptions with pictographic signs costs Rs 4 lakh a year. The team can fund one excavation season plus whole years of the project, or the project alone.
(a) Which source type does the tools-and-fossils site mainly give, and which kind of fact will it not give?
(b) After one excavation season, how many whole project years can the remaining money pay for, and how much is left?
(c) Should the team do the excavation season plus the project, or the project alone for as long as the money lasts? Take a side and name what is given up, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Artefacts and fossils (material remains), which rebuild ways of living but make thoughts, ideas and names hard to know. (b) 12 minus 7.5 is 4.5 lakh, which pays for 1 whole project year (4 lakh) and leaves Rs 0.5 lakh. (c) Either side with a reason. Excavation plus 1 year gives more material remains and starts the script work; the project alone gives 3 years (12 divided by 4) for a script the chapter says is still undeciphered, which could unlock names, events and dates, but gives up new artefacts.
s: (a) Material remains as the source, with thoughts or names as the gap
(b) 4.5 lakh, 1 whole year and Rs 0.5 lakh left
(c) A side taken, with the fact given up named from the chapter

questions.q: A museum label beside a clay tablet reads: 'The tablet records the year of the king's coronation and a war fought in the same decade.' Which feature of the period after writing does the label show?
questions.a: Dating of cultures and events becomes relatively accurate. The chapter says written documents mention specific dates of events such as coronations and wars, so dating becomes relatively accurate. The other options describe the period before writing.
o: Dating of cultures and events becomes relatively accurate
Dating of events remains only approximate, as in earlier ages
Tools are the only source for rebuilding people's lives
The thoughts of people are as hard to know as before

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The dating of events and cultures before writing is only approximate.
Reason (R): No written documents from that period exist to mention the specific dates of events such as coronations or wars.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter links accurate dating after writing to documents that mention dates of events. Where there are none, historians depend on material remains, so dating stays approximate, and R gives the reason for A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Rohan says, 'The Harappan script appears on seals and pottery, so we already know exactly what the Harappans thought and how they ruled.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the Harappan script is pictographic but has not yet been deciphered, so the writing cannot yet be read. Without a deciphered script, Harappan life has to be rebuilt from artefacts, and thoughts and ideas are hard to know from them.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The script has not yet been deciphered
So only material remains are available and thoughts stay hard to know

questions.q: A student lists two developments: (i) australopithecines becoming Homo sapiens, and (ii) humans making tools and techniques to use natural resources as the climate changed. (a) Label each as biological or cultural evolution. (b) Which of the two would an archaeologist read from changes in skull shape, and which from tools lying beside the bones?
questions.a: (a) (i) is biological evolution; (ii) is cultural evolution. (b) Skull changes show biological evolution; the tools beside the bones show cultural evolution.
s: (a) Both developments classified correctly
(b) Skulls linked to biological and tools linked to cultural evolution

questions.q: The Quaternary Period is given as the last 26 lakh years. In millions of years this is ___ million years.

A museum wants a wall 12 metres long to show 3 million years of human history, with the whole wall standing for the span from 3 million years ago to the present. On this scale 1 metre stands for 250,000 years. The curator wants visitors to be able to read a panel about the last 5000 years.
(a) How long, in centimetres, will the last 5000 years be on the wall?
(b) Which of the chapter's two periods fills nearly all of the wall, and which kind of source will visitors see most of?
(c) The designer may keep the true scale or enlarge the last 5000 years to half a metre. Choose one and defend it, saying what visitors will gain and what they may wrongly believe.
questions.a: (a) 5000 divided by 250,000 is 0.02 m, which is 2 cm. (b) The period before writing (more than 99 per cent of history), where tools and other artefacts are the main source. (c) Either choice with a reason. True scale keeps the chapter's point that more than 99 per cent is before writing, but a 2 cm strip cannot show literature and dates; the enlarged half metre (which would stand for 125,000 years if drawn to scale) lets visitors read about written sources but may wrongly suggest the later period is a big share of history.
s: (a) 2 cm
(b) The period before writing, with artefacts as the main source
(c) A choice defended, with a gain and a wrong belief named

questions.q: A student says, 'If human history is taken as about 3 million years, the last 5000 years are less than 1 per cent of it.' About what share are they?
questions.a: About 0.17 per cent, so the chapter's claim holds. 5000 divided by 3,000,000 is about 0.0017, or 0.17 per cent, which is less than 1 per cent.
o: About 0.17 per cent, so the chapter's claim holds
About 1.7 per cent, so the chapter's claim fails
About 17 per cent, so the chapter's claim fails
About 0.017 per cent, so the claim is far too weak

questions.q: Name the main source of information for each of the two periods, before and after the invention of writing, and state what the chapter says is hard to know in the earlier one.
questions.a: Before writing the main source is tools, implements and other material objects (artefacts); after writing literature (written documents) is a main source alongside material remains. In the earlier period it is generally difficult to understand people's thoughts and ideas.
s: Artefacts before writing and written documents after
Thoughts and ideas are difficult to know before writing

questions.q: Write a short account of one object found at a pre-writing site, and show how an archaeologist would use it. Then state one thing about the people that the object alone cannot tell her.
questions.a: Example: a stone handaxe found with animal bones. It shows that the people made and used tools and what they might have cut. It cannot tell her what the people believed or what their leaders were called, because thoughts and names are known from literature.
s: A believable object and where it is found
What it shows about ways of living
A limit: thoughts, ideas or names cannot be read from it

questions.q: Three scripts flourished at about the same time: the Harappan, the cuneiform of Mesopotamia and the hieroglyphic of Egypt. Why does the chapter name only the last two as marking the beginning of the historical period, about 5000 years ago?
questions.a: Those two scripts have been deciphered, but the Harappan has not. The chapter says that, unlike the Harappan script, the cuneiform and hieroglyphic scripts have been deciphered and mark the beginning of the historical period.
o: Those two scripts have been deciphered, but the Harappan has not
Only those two were used on clay or papyrus, whereas Harappan signs were cut on seals and pottery
Only those two were invented before the Harappan script came into use
Only those two were used by farming communities in river plains

questions.q: Compare the period before writing with the period after it under four heads: share of human history, main source, knowledge of people's lives and measurement of time. Then say, giving a reason, which period can tell us more about what people thought.
questions.a: Share: before writing is more than 99 per cent (about 3 million years ago to 5000 years ago); after is less than 1 per cent (the last 5000 years). Main source: artefacts before; material remains and written documents after. Lives: before, ways of living are rebuilt from tools but thoughts and ideas are hard to understand; after, literature gives names, events and social, political and cultural life. Time: approximate before; relatively accurate after. The period after writing tells more about thoughts, because literature carries names, events and cultural life.
s: Share of history for both periods
Main source for both periods
Knowledge of lives for both periods
Measurement of time for both periods
Judgement on thoughts with a reason

questions.q: Which question about a people who left no writing would tools and fossils alone find hardest to answer?
questions.a: What did they believe, and what were the names of their leaders? The chapter says that where there is no writing it is generally difficult to understand people's thoughts and ideas, while literature gives names, events and social, political and cultural life. Tools do show ways of living.
o: What did they believe, and what were the names of their leaders?
How did they make and shape their stone tools from the rocks around them?
Which animals did they hunt or eat, judging from the bones?
Did they live in one region, or move across land over time?

questions.q:
Match each script with what the chapter says about it.
1. Harappan script
2. Cuneiform
3. Hieroglyphic script
4. Brahmi
a. Used from about 400 BCE in southern India and the Ganga Valley
b. Pictographic signs on seals and pottery, not yet deciphered
c. Script of the Sumerians in Mesopotamia, since deciphered
d. Script of ancient Egypt, since deciphered
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-a. The pairs are: Harappan script with Pictographic signs on seals and pottery, not yet deciphered; Cuneiform with Script of the Sumerians in Mesopotamia, since deciphered; Hieroglyphic script with Script of ancient Egypt, since deciphered; Brahmi with Used from about 400 BCE in southern India and the Ganga Valley.

questions.q: The chapter takes the period before writing to run from about 3 million years ago to 5000 years ago. (a) How many lakh years is that period? (b) Show with a calculation whether the last 5000 years are really under 1 per cent of 3 million years.
questions.a: (a) 3,000,000 minus 5,000 is 2,995,000 years, which is 29.95 lakh years. (b) 5000 divided by 3,000,000 is about 0.17 per cent, which is below 1 per cent, so the chapter's claim holds.
s: (a) 2,995,000 years converted to 29.95 lakh years
(b) 0.17 per cent, so below 1 per cent

questions.q:
Read the statements about human evolution in the chapter.
1. Cultural evolution means the gradual physical and genetic change from early ancestors to modern humans.
2. The Quaternary Period, in which cultural evolution is placed, covers the last 26 lakh years including the present.
3. Australopithecines, the early ancestors in the chapter, evolved into modern human beings called Homo sapiens.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: that is biological evolution. Cultural evolution explains how humans adapted by developing tools, techniques and technology. Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
2 only

questions.q: Suppose the Harappan script is deciphered tomorrow. Using the chapter's comparison of the periods before and after writing, say what new kinds of information historians could expect, and what they would still not be able to learn. Justify your answer.
questions.a: The chapter says written documents give names, events and social, political and cultural life, and mention specific dates of events such as coronations and wars. So a deciphered script could give historians Harappan names, events, rulers' dates and details of society. It would not cover everything: the chapter notes that material remains remain a source for how people lived, and writing only records what its writers chose to mention. Dating of the events the writing mentions would become relatively accurate.
s: Names, events and social, political or cultural life from literature
Specific dates of events and relatively accurate dating
A named limit: what writing does not cover and artefacts must supply
Link of the claim to the chapter's before and after table
A justified overall judgement

questions.q: True or False: Once writing began, material remains stopped being a source for rebuilding the lives of people. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that in the later period both material remains and written documents are sources for reconstructing the lives of people and society. Writing added a source; it did not remove the older one.
s: Verdict: False
Reason from the chapter, with the corrected statement

questions.q: Explain, with two points from the chapter, why dating events is easier and more accurate for the period after writing than before it.
questions.a: Written documents mention specific dates of events such as coronations and wars, which gives fixed points. Literature also gives names and events, so historians can place one event after another. Before writing, dating cultures and events is only approximate.
s: Documents mention specific dates such as coronations and wars
Literature gives names and events that can be placed in order
Before writing dating is only approximate

questions.q: (a) From about when, and in which two regions, was the Brahmi script used? (b) The chapter says the Emperor Ashoka formalised it in the 3rd century BCE. Work out how many years after its first use that was, at the earliest and the latest.
questions.a: (a) From about 400 BCE in parts of southern India and the Ganga Valley. (b) The 3rd century BCE runs from 300 to 201 BCE, so Ashoka's formalising came about 100 to 199 years after 400 BCE: roughly one to two centuries.
s: (a) 400 BCE; southern India and the Ganga Valley
(b) Between about 100 and 199 years later

questions.q: A teacher says, 'Tools tell us more about our ancestors than fossils do.' Discuss the claim using what the chapter says each kind of evidence shows. Then give your own judgement.
questions.a: Tools show behaviour: the chapter says stone tool making marks human behaviour, handaxes and cleavers show the technology of Homo erectus, and archaeologists make and use similar tools to learn how objects were created and used. Fossils preserve the body: skulls show the evolutionary sequence from Homo habilis to Homo sapiens, with a gradual straightening of the face. Neither alone is enough. Tools cannot show what a body looked like; fossils cannot show what the person made. A sound judgement says each answers a different question, so the claim is only partly true.
s: What tools show, with the chapter's example
What fossils show, with the chapter's example
A limit of tools
A limit of fossils
A justified judgement on the claim

questions.q: A student lists ways archaeologists learn how early ancestors lived. Which item on her list is wrong, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Reading the early ancestors' own diaries kept in a script of their time. The chapter names excavation of tools and bones, fossils, and experiments with similar tools. Early ancestors left no writing, so no diary of theirs exists.
o: Reading the early ancestors' own diaries kept in a script of their time
Digging up tools, bones and other objects at early sites for clues
Studying fossils preserved from the distant past, found in the earth
Making and using tools like the old ones themselves, to test them

questions.q: True or False: The chapter treats every human ancestor as a tool maker, while crediting only Homo sapiens with complex technologies. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. It says all human ancestors were tool makers, and that it was Homo sapiens that developed complex technologies.
s: Verdict: True
Reason from the chapter

questions.q: On a school trip a guide says, 'Handaxes and cleavers like these have turned up in Asia and in Europe.' Which conclusion fits the chapter?
questions.a: Their makers began in Africa and spread beyond it between 2 and 0.5 million years ago. The chapter says Homo erectus, the maker of handaxes and cleavers, was the first hominin to exit Africa, and that tools found in Asia and Europe show their origin in Africa and dispersion beyond it between 2 and 0.5 million years ago.
o: Their makers began in Africa and spread beyond it between 2 and 0.5 million years ago
Their makers evolved separately in Asia and Europe at the same time as in Africa
Their makers were Homo sapiens leaving Africa about 125,000 years ago
Their makers were Homo habilis who never left the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania and Kenya

questions.q: A student says some handaxes found in Asia were made by Homo sapiens walking out of Africa 125,000 years ago. Show, with the dates in the chapter, why this cannot be accepted for the handaxes and cleavers the chapter discusses.
questions.a: The chapter dates the dispersal of Homo erectus, the makers of handaxes and cleavers, to between 2 and 0.5 million years ago, which is 2,000,000 to 500,000 years. A date of 125,000 years ago is far more recent than 500,000 years ago, so the handaxes of that dispersal cannot belong to the Homo sapiens wave.
s: The handaxes belong to Homo erectus, dispersing 2 to 0.5 million years ago
125,000 years ago is later than 500,000 years ago
Conclusion that the two cannot be the same event

questions.q:
Read the statements about human ancestors.
1. Homo habilis lived in Africa, especially in the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania and Kenya.
2. Homo habilis, and not Homo erectus, was the first hominin to exit Africa.
3. All human ancestors were tool makers, but it was Homo sapiens that developed complex technologies.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says Homo erectus, the inventor of handaxes and cleavers, was among the first to migrate out of Africa. Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
3 only

questions.q: (a) By how many years did Homo erectus's exit from Africa (about 2 million years ago) come after the earliest stone tools (about 3.3 million years ago)? (b) Homo sapiens evolved about 300,000 years ago and left about 125,000 years ago. How many times longer was the gap in (a) than the gap between these two dates?
questions.a: (a) 3,300,000 minus 2,000,000 is 1,300,000 years. (b) 300,000 minus 125,000 is 175,000 years; 1,300,000 divided by 175,000 is about 7.4, so the first gap was about 7.4 times longer.
s: (a) 1.3 million years
(b) 175,000 years and a ratio of about 7.4

questions.q: Meena says, 'A handaxe is only a stone, so calling it a limb makes no sense.' Which reply uses the chapter's reasoning?
questions.a: It extends the body, letting a person do what hands alone cannot. The chapter calls tools 'extra-corporal limbs' because they functioned as extensions of the human body, helping people perform tasks they could not accomplish with their hands alone.
o: It extends the body, letting a person do what hands alone cannot
It grows from the body, as a hand does, and is never discarded
It was made by animals and then taken up by hominins as a gift
It is the fossil of a hand that turned into stone over a long time

questions.q:
A town museum has one empty glass case and two objects to show for its 'How we know about our ancestors' gallery: a replica Homo erectus handaxe with a cleaver, or a cast of the skull series from Homo habilis to Homo sapiens. The curator says the case should teach visitors one main idea.
(a) Which kind of clue does each object represent, and which hominin does the handaxe point to?
(b) The earliest known stone tool is placed about 3.3 million years ago and the handaxe maker's exit from Africa about 2 million years ago. Work out how much older the earliest tool is.
(c) Choose one object for the case. Say what visitors will learn from it and what they will not learn.
questions.a: (a) The handaxe and cleaver are tools made by Homo erectus; the skulls are fossils showing the evolutionary sequence. (b) 3.3 minus 2 is 1.3 million years older. (c) Either choice with a trade-off. Handaxe and cleaver: visitors learn about tool making and the move out of Africa but not what ancestors looked like. Skulls: visitors see a gradual straightening of the face but learn nothing about how the ancestors lived or worked.
s: (a) Tools and fossils identified, with Homo erectus named
(b) 1.3 million years
(c) A choice with what visitors learn and miss

questions.q: (a) Name the type of tool that the chapter's captions link to Homo habilis and the types linked to Homo erectus. (b) Which of the two is said to have left Africa, and what does the finding of such tools in Asia and Europe indicate?
questions.a: (a) Homo habilis: chopper stone tools; Homo erectus: handaxes and cleavers. (b) Homo erectus. Tools of that kind in Asia and Europe indicate an African origin and dispersal beyond Africa between 2 and 0.5 million years ago.
s: (a) Choppers for Homo habilis; handaxes and cleavers for Homo erectus
(b) Homo erectus, with African origin and dispersal shown by the tools

questions.q: A student holds an old stone scraper and a preserved bone from the same layer and says, 'Both are fossils because both are very old.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: Only the bone's remains, traces or impressions qualify as a fossil. The chapter defines a fossil as the preserved remains, traces or impressions of plants, animals or humans. A made stone tool is an object of the past, which the chapter lists separately from fossils as another clue.
o: Only the bone's remains, traces or impressions qualify as a fossil
Neither can be a fossil, since fossils are only of plants
Both are fossils, since the chapter defines fossils by their age alone
Only the scraper is a fossil, since it was shaped by a hominin

questions.q: Explain, with two points from the chapter, why early stone tools are called 'extra-corporal limbs' and why discarded tools help archaeologists today.
questions.a: Tools extended the human body and helped people perform tasks they could not do with their hands alone, so they act like limbs outside the body. Humans made, used and discarded them when they wore out; the discarded tools were buried in the upper layers of earth and later discovered, so they are major evidence for how ancestors lived.
s: Tools extended the body and did tasks hands alone could not
Tools were discarded when worn out and buried in layers of earth
Discovered tools are evidence for reconstructing how ancestors lived

questions.q: A student writes, 'Homo erectus made the first stone tools, 3.3 million years ago.' Using the dates in the chapter, what is wrong with this sentence?
questions.a: The earliest stone tools are about 3.3 million years old, but Homo erectus lived about 2 million years ago, 1.3 million years later. The chapter puts the first tools at about 3.3 million years ago and Homo erectus at about 2 million years ago, so Homo erectus cannot be the first tool maker.
o: The earliest stone tools are about 3.3 million years old, but Homo erectus lived about 2 million years ago, 1.3 million years later
Homo erectus lived about 3.3 million years ago, so the sentence is correct but badly worded
The first stone tools came after Homo erectus had already left Africa for Asia
The first stone tools were made by Homo sapiens about 300,000 years ago in Africa

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The making of the earliest stone tools, about 3.3 million years ago, is described as the beginning of 'human behaviour'.
Reason (R): Animals do not possess the cognitive ability to make such tools.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter sets the making of stone tools against the behaviour of animals, who cannot make them, so R gives the reason the first tools mark human behaviour.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: What does the word 'hominin' cover, and why does the chapter say that making stone tools marked the start of 'human behaviour'?
questions.a: Hominins are a group that includes modern humans and our early human-like ancestors. Making stone tools, which animals lack the cognitive ability to do, marks human behaviour as opposed to animal behaviour.
s: Hominins: modern humans and early human-like ancestors
Tool making needs a cognitive ability that animals do not have

questions.q:
An archaeology club tries to learn how early people used stone tools, as the chapter says archaeologists do. Over the term the club makes 40 replica handaxes at about 45 minutes each, and 15 of them turn out usable. The club has 18 hours left in the term for further work.
(a) Why do archaeologists make and use replica tools, according to the chapter?
(b) How many hours did the 40 attempts take, what share were usable, and how many hours of making does each usable axe cost on average?
(c) The club can spend all 18 hours making more axes, or spend them using the 15 axes it has for cutting and scraping tasks. Choose one and say what the club gains and gives up.
questions.a: (a) To understand how early humans created, used and depended on such objects in daily life. (b) 40 times 45 minutes is 1800 minutes, which is 30 hours; 15 of 40 is 37.5 per cent; 30 hours divided by 15 is 2 hours per usable axe. (c) Either side. More making would give 18 divided by 2, about 9 more axes, but little new understanding of use. Using the 15 axes answers how objects are used, but adds no new axes to compare.
s: (a) Replicas show how objects were created, used and depended on
(b) 30 hours, 37.5 per cent and 2 hours per usable axe
(c) A choice with a gain and a loss named

questions.q: Homo erectus is placed as leaving Africa between 2 and 0.5 million years ago. This window of dispersion lasted ___ million years.
Explain how a discarded stone tool and a buried body each end up as evidence that an archaeologist can study.
questions.a: Tools were made, used and discarded when they wore out; they got buried in the upper layers of earth and were later discovered. Remains of ancestors buried deep underground turned into fossils over thousands or millions of years.
s: Tools: made, used, discarded, buried and later discovered
Bodies: buried deep, turned into fossils over a long time

questions.q: Compare four human ancestors named in the chapter: Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Homo neanderthalensis and Homo sapiens. For each give where they lived or went and what they are linked to, and then say which of them is the only one still living.
questions.a: Homo habilis lived in Africa, especially the Olduvai Gorge, and made chopper stone tools. Homo erectus lived in the Eastern African Rift Valley about 2 million years ago, made handaxes and cleavers and spread into Europe and Asia. Homo neanderthalensis lived in Europe and Southwest Asia till about 40,000 years ago and made Middle Palaeolithic flake tools. Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago, moved out about 125,000 years ago and developed complex technologies; living humans are the only human species alive today.
s: Homo habilis with place and tools
Homo erectus with place, tools and spread
Homo neanderthalensis with place and tools
Homo sapiens with origin, movement and technology
The only living species named correctly

questions.q: Anil says, 'Homo sapiens were the first to leave Africa, about 125,000 years ago.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter does say that a major wave of movement out of Africa about 125,000 years ago was associated with early Homo sapiens, who evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago. But Homo erectus left earlier, about 2 million years ago, so Homo sapiens were not the first.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right part: the wave about 125,000 years ago was Homo sapiens
The wrong part: Homo erectus left about 2 million years ago

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says that rock painting and ornament making began only after humans took to farming in the Neolithic. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says later Palaeolithic hunters decorated cave and rock-shelter walls, used pigments on their bodies and were the first to produce beads of stone, bone and shell, and that art flourished in the Mesolithic. All this came before farming.
s: Verdict: False
Reason from the chapter, with the corrected statement

questions.q: Why does the chapter say the Mesolithic world saw the first-ever population explosion in human history?
questions.a: A warmer climate brought forests, grasslands, small game, fish and wild grains. The chapter says that about 12,000 years ago the climate became warmer, forests and grasslands spread to former ice-covered areas, and these landscapes offered small game, fish and edible wild grains. Farming, copper and domestication belong to later stages.
o: A warmer climate brought forests, grasslands, small game, fish and wild grains
The shift to farming gave people a surplus of wheat and barley to store
Copper tools made hunting easier and food more abundant for every band
Domesticated cattle gave a steady supply of milk and meat all through the year

questions.q: Compare the earlier Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers with the Mesolithic hunter-gatherers under four heads: tools, food, art and habitat. Then give your judgement on whether the Mesolithic was a break from the earlier way of life or a step on from it, using the chapter's description of it as a transitional phase.
questions.a: Tools: earlier large cutting tools such as handaxes and cleavers and later smaller scrapers, borers and points; Mesolithic microlithic tools. Food: earlier meat, tubers and marrow, small game later; Mesolithic fish, small game and wild grains, fishing the mainstay. Art: earlier cave paintings, body pigments and beads; Mesolithic art flourished. Habitat: earlier caves and rock shelters; Mesolithic caves and rock shelters were frequently occupied. Judgement: the chapter calls the Mesolithic a transitional phase between hunting-gathering and agriculture, and it still depended on hunting, fishing and gathering, so it was a step on, not a break.
s: Tools compared
Food compared
Art compared
Habitat compared
Judgement using the transitional-phase idea

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Stone Age in the chapter.
1. The word palaeo means 'old' and lithic means 'stone', so the Palaeolithic is also known as the Old Stone Age.
2. Mesolithic people depended mainly on farming, with fishing only a minor activity.
3. A burin or engraver was a hunting weapon used for thrusting into large animals.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. Statement 2 is false: fishing was the mainstay of the Mesolithic subsistence economy. Statement 3 is false: a burin was used to engrave symbolic features on bones and shells such as ostrich eggs. Statement 1 is from the chapter.
o: 1 only
1, 2 and 3
3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: The oldest human settlement in the subcontinent is dated to about 2 million years ago and Isampur to 1.2 million years ago. (a) How many years older is the oldest settlement than Isampur? (b) The Mesolithic is placed about 12,000 years ago. How many times older is the oldest settlement than the Mesolithic, correct to one decimal place?
questions.a: (a) 2,000,000 minus 1,200,000 is 800,000 years, or 8 lakh years. (b) 2,000,000 divided by 12,000 is about 166.7 times.
s: (a) 8 lakh years
(b) About 166.7 times

questions.q:
Two hunter-gatherer camps lie in the same valley. Camp A has 120 handaxes and cleavers and 10 microblades. Camp B has 15 handaxes and cleavers, 135 microblades, bone points and many fish bones. A team can deepen the digging at only one camp this season.
(a) Which camp is likely the later one, and which chapter feature supports this?
(b) What share of the stone tools at each camp are microblades, to the nearest tenth of a per cent?
(c) Choose which camp to dig deeper and say what the team will learn and what it will miss.
questions.a: (a) Camp B, because microlithic tools and fishing mark the Mesolithic, a later stage than the age of large cutting tools. (b) Camp A: 10 divided by 130 is about 7.7 per cent; Camp B: 135 divided by 150 is 90.0 per cent. (c) Either choice. Camp A would give more about early large-tool hunting; Camp B would show fishing and the transition, with the earlier stage thinly represented.
s: (a) Camp B, with microlithic tools and fishing as the reason
(b) 7.7 per cent and 90.0 per cent
(c) A choice with a gain and a loss named

questions.q: An archaeologist working in a rock shelter records tiny stone blades fixed in handles, fish bones, painted walls and signs of repeated occupation, but no evidence of farming. Which stage of the Stone Age does the chapter link to this combination?
questions.a: Mesolithic, with microlithic tools and fishing as the mainstay. Microlithic tools, fishing as the mainstay, flourishing art and frequently occupied caves and rock shelters are the chapter's Mesolithic features; Neolithic and Chalcolithic stages involve farming or copper.
o: Mesolithic, with microlithic tools and fishing as the mainstay
Palaeolithic, with large handaxes as the only tools in use at the time
Neolithic, with domesticated animals and village houses of sun-dried brick
Chalcolithic, with copper used along with stone tools in the settlements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Microlithic tools helped Mesolithic people gather aquatic food, both marine and freshwater.
Reason (R): Art flourished in the Mesolithic period and new habitats such as caves and rock shelters were frequently occupied.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both statements are in the chapter, but the flourishing of art and the occupation of caves does not explain how people were able to gather aquatic food. The tools did.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Ruchi says, 'The first population explosion in human history came when the climate warmed about 12,000 years ago.' Test her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the warmer climate opened up forests and grasslands with small game, fish and wild grains, and that the world then witnessed the first-ever population explosion. Her claim matches the chapter, including the date of about 12,000 years ago.
s: Verdict: the claim is right
Warming gave forests, grasslands and more food resources
The chapter names the first-ever population explosion at that time

questions.q: (a) Name the three main types of smaller stone tools the chapter lists after the large cutting tools. (b) Which later inventions did the hunters of this period add, and what kind of animal did they now also hunt?
questions.a: (a) Scrapers, borers and points. (b) The bow and arrow, and parallel-sided blade and microblade tools; they also hunted small game animals.
s: (a) Scrapers, borers and points
(b) Bow and arrow with blade tools; small game hunted

questions.q: A Class 9 student studies the tool kit of later Palaeolithic hunters: scrapers, borers and points. What does the chapter say these smaller tools show about hunting?
questions.a: Hunting became more efficient through projectiles tipped with sharp points. The chapter says the main types of smaller stone tools were scrapers, borers and points, which indicate improved efficiency in hunting by developing projectiles tipped with sharp points.
o: Hunting became more efficient through projectiles tipped with sharp points
Hunting was given up in favour of farming on the banks of rivers and lakes nearby
Hunters now depended only on fishing and on gathering wild grains
Hunters used only large handaxes and cleavers to cut up the meat

questions.q:
A state wants to open a painted rock-shelter site to visitors. It has 180 painted shelters with Mesolithic and earlier occupation. A protective railing and cover cost Rs 30,000 per shelter, and the state has set aside Rs 40 lakh. Any shelter without a railing must stay closed to visitors.
(a) What features of the shelters connect them to the Mesolithic way of life as the chapter describes it?
(b) How many shelters can be given railings, and how many must stay closed?
(c) The state can either put railings on as many shelters as the money allows and close the rest, or spread the money thinly to open all 180 with only ropes. Choose one plan and say what heritage or public access is lost.
questions.a: (a) Painted walls (art flourished) and caves and rock shelters that were frequently occupied. (b) 180 times 30,000 is Rs 54 lakh, so the budget of Rs 40 lakh covers 4,000,000 divided by 30,000 = 133 shelters (rounded down); 180 minus 133 gives 47 shelters closed. (c) Either choice. The cluster plan protects 133 painted shelters but keeps 47 closed; the rope plan gives access to all but leaves the paintings open to damage.
s: (a) Painted walls and occupied shelters linked to the Mesolithic
(b) 133 protected and 47 closed
(c) A choice with the loss named

questions.q: The chapter says Homo sapiens spread over the world, including Australia and the Americas, between 50,000 and 12,000 years ago. This spread took about ___ years.
Write a short find-list for a rock shelter that an archaeologist would label Mesolithic, naming four finds, and say what each find tells her about how the people lived.
questions.a: Example: microblades fixed in handles (microlithic tools), fish bones (fishing as the mainstay), painted walls (art flourished) and signs of repeated use (caves and rock shelters occupied often). Together they show a hunter-gatherer life based on fishing and small game.
s: Four finds true to the Mesolithic
Each linked to a way of living
A concluding link to hunter-gatherer life with fishing

questions.q: Which of these finds would NOT fit a Mesolithic site, according to the chapter's account of the Stone Age stages?
questions.a: Bones of domesticated sheep penned near a village and polished stone tools. The chapter's chart lists domestication of animals and polished stone tools as Neolithic features. The other finds fit Mesolithic microlithic tools, fishing and art.
o: Bones of domesticated sheep penned near a village and polished stone tools
Microlithic blades together with fish bones and bone points at the camp
Painted walls in a cave or rock shelter that people used again and again
Evidence that fishing was the main way of getting food for the whole group

questions.q: Trace how the stone tool kit of the Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers improved, from the large cutting tools at sites like Attirampakkam to the blades and engraving tools. For each stage say what the new tool made possible, and state which people the chapter associates with the latest developments.
questions.a: Large cutting tools, handaxes, cleavers, scrapers and choppers, were used to chop meat, dig out tubers, scrape skins and cleave bones for marrow. Smaller scrapers, borers and points improved hunting efficiency through tipped projectiles. Later the bow and arrow and parallel-sided blades and microblades allowed hunting of small game; the burin engraved symbols on bones and shells; and microblades fixed in handles were easier to use. The chapter associates the latest developments with our immediate ancestors, Homo sapiens, who spread over the world including Australia and the Americas.
s: Large cutting tools with uses
Smaller tools with the hunting gain
Bow and arrow and blades with their gain
Burin and handles with their use
Homo sapiens named as the people linked to the later stage

questions.q: (a) By about how many years ago did the climate become warmer, and what happened to the land that ice sheets had covered? (b) Name two food resources the new landscapes offered and say which one became the mainstay of the economy.
questions.a: (a) About 12,000 years ago; forests and grasslands expanded into areas that were previously covered by ice sheets. (b) Any two of small game animals, fish and edible wild grains; fishing became the mainstay of the subsistence economy.
s: (a) About 12,000 years ago, with forests and grasslands expanding
(b) Two resources named, with fishing as the mainstay

questions.q:
Match each site or idea with the detail the chapter gives.
1. Attirampakkam
2. Isampur
3. Bhimbetka
4. Subsistence in the Mesolithic
a. In Karnataka, dated to 1.2 million years ago
b. In Tamil Nadu, dated to about 1.5-1.7 million years ago
c. In Madhya Pradesh, with hundreds of painted rock shelters
d. Fishing was the mainstay
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. The pairs are: Attirampakkam with In Tamil Nadu, dated to about 1.5-1.7 million years ago; Isampur with In Karnataka, dated to 1.2 million years ago; Bhimbetka with In Madhya Pradesh, with hundreds of painted rock shelters; Subsistence in the Mesolithic with Fishing was the mainstay.

questions.q: Explain three links in the chain by which the warming of the Earth about 12,000 years ago changed how people lived.
questions.a: Warmer climate allowed forests and grasslands to spread where ice sheets had been. These landscapes offered small game, fish and edible wild grains, which supported the first population explosion. Microlithic tools let people gather aquatic food, so fishing became the mainstay, and caves and rock shelters were frequently occupied.
s: Warming and spread of forests and grasslands
New foods and a population explosion
Microlithic tools, fishing and occupation of shelters

questions.q: Differentiate the stone tools of the large-cutting-tool phase from the microlithic tools of the Mesolithic, naming one example of each and one use the chapter gives.
questions.a: Large cutting tools such as handaxes and cleavers were used to chop meat, cleave bones for marrow and so on; microlithic tools were tiny stone tools, such as microblades fixed in handles, that let people gather aquatic food and fish.
s: Large cutting tools with an example and a use
Microlithic tools with an example and a use

questions.q:
Match each term with what the chapter says about it.
1. Domestication
2. Chalcolithic
3. Mehrgarh
4. Neolithic farmers' tools
a. Use of copper along with stone tools
b. Bringing select animals and plants under human control
c. Oldest Neolithic site, on the Bolan River
d. Made for food production and processing
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. The pairs are: Domestication with Bringing select animals and plants under human control; Chalcolithic with Use of copper along with stone tools; Mehrgarh with Oldest Neolithic site, on the Bolan River; Neolithic farmers' tools with Made for food production and processing.

questions.q: A dig reveals sun-dried brick houses, granaries, graves, grains of wheat and barley and the bones of sheep, goats and humped cattle, but no metal objects. Which description matches the chapter's picture of Mehrgarh at its earliest?
questions.a: An agricultural village of about 7000 BCE, the oldest Neolithic site named. The chapter dates the earliest agricultural village at Mehrgarh to about 7000 BCE. Its houses, granaries, graves, crops and herds fit the Neolithic way of life; copper objects came later.
o: An agricultural village of about 7000 BCE, the oldest Neolithic site named
A copper-using village of about 4000 BCE that had given up farming altogether
A Mesolithic camp that depended on fishing and on tiny microlith tools
A Bronze Age city of about 3500 BCE with mature town planning and seals

questions.q: Give two ways, from the chapter, in which the life of Neolithic farmers differed from that of hunter-gatherers.
questions.a: Any two of: they made tools for food production and processing and not just for procuring food; they made earthenware pottery in various shapes and sizes; they established the first village settlements; they domesticated animals and plants.
s: First difference with a chapter detail
Second difference with a chapter detail

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Neolithic revolution took place at the same time all over the world.
Reason (R): The chart in the chapter shows that the transition to agriculture took place at different periods in different areas.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. A is false because the chapter says the transition did not occur at the same time everywhere. R is a true statement of what the chart shows.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
A village of 60 families in a Mehrgarh-like setting stores grain in a granary that holds 12,000 kg. Each family needs 240 kg of grain a year. The village can raise more sheep and goats, or build a small second granary holding 2,400 kg if ten families give up a month of work.
(a) Which feature of Mehrgarh does the granary correspond to, and what does farming allow that hunting does not?
(b) How many kilograms of grain does the village need, and how many families' needs are not covered?
(c) Should the village raise more sheep and goats to cover the gap, or have ten families grow more grain and build the small granary to store it? Choose, and name the risk you accept.
questions.a: (a) The granaries of Mehrgarh; farming allows food to be stored from one harvest to the next because crops are cultivated under human control. (b) 60 times 240 is 14,400 kg, which is 2,400 kg more than 12,000 kg; 2,400 divided by 240 means 10 families are not covered. (c) Either choice with the risk. More sheep and goats use the animals the chapter says Mehrgarh raised but need care; more grain relies on the harvest.
s: (a) Granaries identified, with storing food from cultivation
(b) 14,400 kg, a gap of 2,400 kg and 10 families
(c) A choice with the risk accepted

questions.q: Which statement about the Neolithic transition is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: It began at the same time in every region of the world. The chapter says the chart shows the transition did not occur at the same time everywhere but at different periods in different areas.
o: It began at the same time in every region of the world
It was a gradual move from hunting and gathering to food production
It took place at different periods in different areas
It led to the first village settlements in several regions

questions.q: (a) How many years passed between the earliest agricultural village at Mehrgarh (about 7000 BCE) and the people's entering the metal age (by about 4000 BCE)? (b) The chapter says this laid the basis for the Bronze Age Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation around 3500 BCE. How many years is the whole journey from the village to the civilisation?
questions.a: (a) 7000 minus 4000 is 3,000 years. (b) 4000 minus 3500 is a further 500 years, so the whole journey is 3,000 plus 500, which is 3,500 years.
s: (a) 3,000 years
(b) 500 more years, 3,500 in all

questions.q: Write a short scene of one day in a Neolithic village like Mehrgarh. Include three details from the chapter and one challenge the farmer would face that a hunter-gatherer would not.
questions.a: Example: Before sunrise a farmer collects wheat from a granary, feeds the sheep and goats, then makes a pot. Details: wheat and barley, sheep and goats, granaries or earthenware pottery. A challenge: she must tend crops and herds through the seasons and store grain, whereas a hunter-gatherer simply moves to food.
s: Three details true to the chapter
A believable day
A challenge specific to farming life

questions.q: The chapter places Mehrgarh's earliest agricultural village at about 7000 BCE and says its people were Chalcolithic by about 4000 BCE. About how long did that move from farming village to copper-using people take?
questions.a: About 3,000 years. 7000 BCE minus 4000 BCE is 3,000 years; 3,500 years is the gap to the civilisation of around 3500 BCE.
o: About 3,000 years
About 300 years
About 3,500 years
About 11,000 years

questions.q:
A site has three layers. The oldest has microblades and fish bones. The middle layer has granaries, earthenware pottery, wheat grains and the bones of sheep and goats. The newest layer has copper beads found with stone tools. The team dates the middle layer to about 7000 BCE and the newest to about 4000 BCE. The team can publish only one headline.
(a) Name the stage of each layer.
(b) For how many years did the middle stage last before copper appeared, on these dates?
(c) Headline X: 'This site shows the whole journey from hunting-fishing to metal.' Headline Y: 'This site is another Mehrgarh.' Choose one and say what extra evidence would settle your choice.
questions.a: (a) Oldest: Mesolithic; middle: Neolithic; newest: Chalcolithic. (b) 7000 minus 4000 is 3,000 years. (c) Either with a reason. X fits the three stages; it needs layers that show them in unbroken order. Y compares with Mehrgarh, which the chapter dates to about 7000 BCE and places on the Bolan River; it would need matching features such as zebu bones, sun-dried brick houses, graves and shell ornaments.
s: (a) Mesolithic, Neolithic and Chalcolithic named in order
(b) 3,000 years
(c) A headline chosen, with evidence that would settle it

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says that Neolithic farmers still made stone tools; what changed was that the tools were now made for producing and processing food. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. It contrasts hunter-gatherers, who produced tools for procuring food, with Neolithic farmers, who made tools for food production and processing, and shows Neolithic stone tools.
s: Verdict: True
Reason from the chapter

questions.q: Treat Mehrgarh as evidence. List five features of the site from the chapter, and for each say what it shows about the Neolithic way of life or the move to the Chalcolithic.
questions.a: Sun-dried brick houses and granaries show settled village life and storage. Graves show a custom of burying the dead. Ornaments of lapis lazuli, carnelian and shells show craft work with varied raw materials. Wheat and barley, and sheep, goats and zebu, show domestication. The first copper objects show entry into the metal age, the Chalcolithic, by about 4000 BCE.
s: Houses and granaries with meaning
Graves with meaning
Ornaments with meaning
Crops and herds with meaning
Copper objects linked to the Chalcolithic

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Neolithic period in the Indian subcontinent.
1. Mehrgarh, the oldest Neolithic site, lies on the Ganga plains where rice was first grown.
2. The people of Mehrgarh lived by hunting alone and had no crops or herds.
3. By 2500 BCE most of the subcontinent was occupied by Neolithic agricultural communities.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. Statement 1 is false: Mehrgarh is on the Bolan River in present-day Pakistan, in the northwest. Statement 2 is false: they cultivated wheat and barley and raised sheep, goats and zebu. Statement 3 is from the chapter.
o: 3 only
2 only
1 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q: Differentiate the Neolithic from the Chalcolithic, giving the main feature of each from the chapter's chart of periods.
questions.a: The Neolithic (New Stone Age) is the shift from hunting-gathering to agriculture and settled life, with domestication of animals and polished stone tools. The Chalcolithic (Copper and Stone Age) is the use of copper along with stone tools and early metallurgy.
s: Neolithic: agriculture, settled life and domestication
Chalcolithic: copper used with stone tools

questions.q: Why does the chapter call the shift from hunting and gathering to farming a 'revolution'?
questions.a: People brought select animals and plants under their control and began village life. The chapter names the hallmark as the domestication of select animals and plants, bringing them under human control, with new breeds through cultivation and husbandry, and says the first village settlements laid the foundations for the urban revolution.
o: People brought select animals and plants under their control and began village life
People stopped using stone tools and began to depend on iron for all their work
People moved into large cities and began writing on clay tablets within a century
People began fishing and hunting small game after the climate grew warmer

questions.q: Explain three ways in which the Neolithic revolution prepared the ground for the later urban revolution.
questions.a: It brought animals and plants under human control, giving a more settled food supply. Farmers established the first village settlements with houses and granaries. They made tools for food production and processing and developed pottery, using a variety of raw materials, which the chapter says laid the foundations for the urban revolution.
s: Domestication and settled food supply
First village settlements
Tools, pottery and raw materials

questions.q: The Sanganakallu Neolithic site is dated to 2000 BCE, which is ___ years after the earliest agricultural village at Mehrgarh (about 7000 BCE).
Hari says, 'Mehrgarh is the oldest Neolithic site, so farming began there before anywhere else in the world.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter calls Mehrgarh the oldest Neolithic site in the Indian subcontinent, and the earliest agricultural village there, dated to about 7000 BCE. It says the transition to farming took place at different periods in different parts of the world, and its chart shows other regions with their own crops. The chapter does not say Mehrgarh was first in the world.
s: Verdict: the claim goes too far
Oldest only in the subcontinent
The transition varied from region to region

questions.q: (a) Name the two crops and the three kinds of animals that the people of Mehrgarh cultivated and raised. (b) Which of these is domestication of plants and which of animals, and why does the chapter call domestication the hallmark of the Neolithic revolution?
questions.a: (a) Wheat and barley; sheep, goats and zebu cattle. (b) Wheat and barley are domesticated plants; sheep, goats and zebu are domesticated animals. Bringing them under human control, with new breeds through cultivation and husbandry, is what made the shift to food production.
s: (a) Wheat and barley; sheep, goats and zebu
(b) Plants and animals sorted correctly, with domestication as the hallmark

questions.q: The chapter asks whether life became easier or more challenging after humans started farming. Give two reasons from the chapter for each side and then take a position.
questions.a: Easier: domesticated plants and animals brought food under human control; granaries and houses gave a settled life. More challenging: farmers had to make tools for food production and processing and keep bringing plants and animals under human control through cultivation and husbandry. Position: either, as long as it uses these reasons, for example that farming was more demanding but gave a more reliable food supply and the basis for villages.
s: Two reasons for easier life
Two reasons for more challenging life
Reasons taken from the chapter
A clear position
A link between the position and the reasons

questions.q: Sara says, 'Copper tools alone caused the prosperity of the Early Harappan communities.' Test her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says that introducing copper tools in the Indus and Ghaggar-Sarasvati plains enhanced productivity and led to prosperity. But it also says the Harappans were not merely agriculturists: pottery was a major craft that boosted their economy, along with copper work, shell work and bead production. So copper was one cause among several.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right part: copper tools raised productivity and prosperity
The missing part: pottery and other crafts also boosted the economy

questions.q: A student writes, 'The Early Harappan stage began after the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation had emerged in 2600 BCE.' Why does the chapter's account contradict this?
questions.a: Early Harappan is the stage of continuity that led to the civilisation by 2600 BCE. The chapter says it looks at the early stages that led to the emergence of the civilisation by 2600 BCE, and describes sites showing cultural continuity as Early Harappan.
o: Early Harappan is the stage of continuity that led to the civilisation by 2600 BCE
Early Harappan is the name the chapter gives to the Late Harappan decline of cities
Early Harappan sites were Neolithic villages and had no pottery or crafts at all
Early Harappan began only in the Iron Age after the mature cities had fallen

questions.q:
Read the statements about water management and early symbols in the chapter.
1. Graffiti on pottery and a few seals with geometric and simple animal motifs from Harappa, Rehman Dheri and Kunal are seen as forerunners to the script and inscribed seals.
2. The Dholavira tanks, made of stone and mud-brick and linked together, took water diverted from a single large river, and none were cut into the bedrock.
3. The huge dockyard at Lothal was built entirely of burnt bricks.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says the Dholavira tanks took water diverted from two nearby streams and some were cut deeper into the bedrock.
o: 1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Three neighbouring villages trade beads and grain. Each village uses its own weights, and disputes over weights cost the traders about Rs 9,000 a year in lost sales. A set of standard stone weights for one village would cost Rs 2,400. Ten elders must agree on one system, and the talks are expected to take most of a year.
(a) What system of weights does the chapter say the Harappans followed, and for which units?
(b) How much would standard sets for all three villages cost, and how many years of dispute losses is that?
(c) Should the villages adopt the standard sets now, or first try the simpler fix of marking each local weight with a common mark? Choose and say what you risk.
questions.a: (a) Binary multiples (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on) for smaller units and multiples of ten for larger ones. (b) 3 times Rs 2,400 is Rs 7,200, which is 0.8 of a year of Rs 9,000 losses. (c) Either choice. Standard sets end disputes for good and support long-distance trade, as the chapter hints, but need the elders' agreement. A common mark is cheaper and quick but may leave real differences in weight.
s: (a) Binary multiples for small and tens for large units
(b) Rs 7,200, 0.8 of a year of losses
(c) A choice with the risk named

questions.q: A Harappan trader weighs small beads with weights of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 units and heavy bales with weights of 100 and 200 units. Which description of the chapter's system fits her weights?
questions.a: Binary multiples for small units and multiples of ten for larger ones. The chapter says the Harappans followed a binary multiple system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on) for smaller units and multiples of ten for larger denominations. The base 60 belongs to the Sumerians.
o: Binary multiples for small units and multiples of ten for larger ones
Multiples of ten for small units and binary multiples for larger ones
Binary multiples at every scale, with no use of tens
Multiples of sixty, as in the Sumerian number system

questions.q: (a) What did the ploughed fields at Kalibangan show? (b) Name the two seasonal crops the chapter compares them with, and say how old the chapter calls this tradition.
questions.a: (a) Horizontal and vertical furrows indicating double crop cultivation. (b) Rabi and Kharif; a tradition nearly 5,000 years old.
s: (a) Furrows in both directions showing double cropping
(b) Rabi and Kharif, nearly 5,000 years old

questions.q: Explain how the technology and economic integration of the Early Harappan period led to the emergence of the urban centres. Use at least four developments from the chapter and end with one sentence on why this stage matters for understanding the civilisation.
questions.a: Copper tools enhanced productivity and prosperity. Large-scale pottery with regional styles, beads, shell work and copper work showed a growing set of crafts. Perimeter walls, seals and the beginnings of the script point to organised settlements. Standard weights and measures supported interregional trade. Water management, from gabarbands to the later Dholavira tanks, supported farming and settlement. Together these technological advancements and economic integration led to the emergence of the civilisation's urban centres, so the stage explains how the civilisation arose and not just how it looked.
s: Copper tools and productivity
Crafts such as pottery, beads and shell work
Walls, seals, script or weights
Water management or trade
A closing statement of why the stage matters

questions.q: A farmer in Kalibangan today ploughs her field in one direction and then crosswise, for a rabi and a kharif crop. Which find does the chapter link to this practice?
questions.a: Ploughed furrows at Kalibangan, horizontal and vertical, indicating double cropping. The chapter shows the ploughed field at Kalibangan with horizontal and vertical furrows indicating double crop cultivation, like the Rabi and Kharif cultivation practised even today.
o: Ploughed furrows at Kalibangan, horizontal and vertical, indicating double cropping
Cubical stone weights, reported from several sites, in binary multiples of one, two and four
Deep tanks cut into the bedrock at Dholavira and joined by channels
A dockyard built entirely of burnt bricks at Lothal, on the coast

questions.q: Using binary-multiple weights of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 units, a load of 45 units can be balanced with 32, 8, 4 and ___ units.
Differentiate the gabarbands of the Early Harappans from the tanks at Dholavira, giving how each handled water.
questions.a: Gabarbands were check dams built across small streams to enhance irrigation. At Dholavira water from two nearby streams was diverted by dams and canals into a series of deep, interconnected tanks built of stone and mud-brick, some cut into bedrock, to conserve water within the site.
s: Gabarbands: check dams across small streams for irrigation
Dholavira: diversion into deep interconnected tanks to conserve water

questions.q: A student lists continuities from Early Harappan into the civilisation. Which item is NOT among those the chapter lists?
questions.a: Planned grid streets with drains in every settlement. The chapter lists continuity in pottery traditions, semi-precious stone beads, shell bangles, terracotta objects and copper working. Grid streets are not listed as a continuity.
o: Planned grid streets with drains in every settlement
Pottery traditions
Semi-precious stone beads and shell bangles
Terracotta objects and copper working

questions.q:
A hillside settlement plans five identical tanks, as at Dholavira, to hold water diverted from two streams. Each tank measures 20 m by 10 m and is 4 m deep. The 500 people use 40 litres each a day. The planners can either deepen every tank by 1 m by cutting into bedrock, at a cost of Rs 6 lakh, or build a sixth tank of the same size, at a cost of Rs 5 lakh. (1 cubic metre holds 1000 litres.)
(a) Which features of the Dholavira system does this plan copy?
(b) For how many days will the five tanks, filled once, supply the village?
(c) Which expansion should the planners choose? Compare the cost for each extra day of water and say what else you would weigh.
questions.a: (a) Diversion of stream water, a series of deep interconnected tanks, and cutting deeper into bedrock. (b) One tank holds 20 times 10 times 4 = 800 cubic metres, so five hold 4,000; the village uses 500 times 40 litres = 20,000 litres = 20 cubic metres a day; 4,000 divided by 20 is 200 days. (c) Deepening adds 1,000 cubic metres, or 50 days, at Rs 12,000 a day; a sixth tank adds 800 cubic metres, or 40 days, at Rs 12,500 a day. Either choice with a reason, such as the slightly lower cost of deepening against the extra site and labour for a new tank.
s: (a) Diverted streams, linked deep tanks or bedrock cutting
(b) 200 days with the working

questions.q:

questions.a: A is false, but R is true. A is false and R is true. The chapter says the furrows ran horizontally and vertically and indicate double cropping, so the claim about one direction and one crop is false.

questions.q: A student says a set of weights of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 units, each used at most once, can balance a load of 40 units. Show that it cannot, and say what the chapter's system adds for larger loads.
questions.a: The total of the set is 1 plus 2 plus 4 plus 8 plus 16, which is 31 units, and 31 is less than 40, so no combination of these weights can reach 40. The chapter's system adds multiples of ten for larger denominations (and further binary multiples such as 32).

31 is less than 40, so no combination can balance it

questions.q: Some radio-carbon dates suggest that the Pre-Harappan phase at Bhirrana and Kunal began between 7000 and 5500 BCE. (a) How many years before the civilisation's emergence by 2600 BCE does that put the start, at the earliest and the latest? (b) How many years before 2600 BCE had copper working been mastered, taking the date given for it?
questions.a: (a) 7000 minus 2600 is 4,400 years and 5500 minus 2600 is 2,900 years, so between 2,900 and 4,400 years before. (b) The chapter gives about 4000 BCE for mastering copper extraction: 4000 minus 2600 is 1,400 years before.
s: (a) Between 2,900 and 4,400 years before
(b) 1,400 years before

questions.q: A teacher compares the Sumerians' canals with the Early Harappans' gabarbands in Baluchistan. What does the chapter say these two had in common?
questions.a: Both were water-management works built to enhance irrigation. The chapter says that while the Sumerians were developing canal irrigation, the Early Harappans were building check dams called gabarbands across small streams to enhance irrigation.
o: Both were water-management works built to enhance irrigation
Both were walls built to protect the cities from raiders and invading armies
Both were ports for loading goods onto boats and unloading them again
Both were tanks cut deep into the bedrock inside a city to hold water

questions.q: Compare the gabarbands, the Dholavira tanks and the Lothal dockyard as examples of Harappan water management, giving for each the place, the material or method and the purpose. Then say which the chapter calls a 'much evolved form' of the earlier skills and why.
questions.a: Gabarbands: check dams across small streams in the foothills of Baluchistan, to enhance irrigation. Dholavira: water from two nearby streams diverted by dams and canals into a series of deep interconnected tanks of stone and mud-brick, some cut into bedrock, to conserve water within the site. Dholavira compared
Lothal compared

A reason for the choice

questions.q: True or False: The perimeter wall around a settlement, the use of seals and the beginnings of the script all appeared for the first time only after the mature cities arose around 2600 BCE. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says these developments probably had their beginnings in the Early Harappan stage, which came before the civilisation emerged by 2600 BCE.
s: Verdict: False
Reason from the chapter, with the corrected statement

questions.q: Explain three ways in which the crafts of the Early Harappan stage show continuity into the civilisation.
questions.a: Pottery traditions continued and the regional styles became standard features by about 2500 BCE. Semi-precious stone beads and shell bangles continued, with bead production found at Harappa, Kunal and Datrana. Terracotta objects and copper working continued too.

Beads and shell bangles with site examples
Terracotta objects and copper working

questions.a: Any two of: building a perimeter wall around the settlement; the use of seals; the Harappan script. Graffiti on pottery and seals with simple motifs at Harappa, Rehman Dheri and Kunal were forerunners to the script and the inscribed seals of the civilisation.

Forerunners named: graffiti on pottery and seals with simple motifs, with a site example

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says the Mesopotamian and Harappan civilisations had strong contacts and trade, partly because they lie closer to each other than to Egypt or China. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. It gives their geographical closeness as the reason for strong contacts and trade, and says Egypt and China have little tangible evidence of direct contact with the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation.
s: Verdict: True
Reason from the chapter

questions.q: A guard at an ancient Sumerian city notes that the high walls have only one entrance, and that the top of the central stepped temple is a holy place that few may enter. Which reason does the chapter give for the single entrance?
questions.a: The central temple also served as the city's treasury. The chapter says the surrounding walls of the ziggurat area had only one entrance because the ziggurat also served as the city's treasury; palaces and royal storehouses lay around it.

The city had no need of trade with other regions or distant lands
The farmers of the city lived inside the walls through the whole year
The gods were believed to guard the canal gates from the temple top

questions.q: Describe two ways in which a Sumerian city's buildings and people reflected a social hierarchy.
questions.a: Kings lived in grand palaces while ordinary people lived in small brick houses. Entry to the sacred temple was restricted to high priests and priestesses, who were probably part of the ruling class.
s: Palaces against small brick houses
Temple entry restricted to priests and priestesses

questions.q: Describe a Sumerian city under these heads: its main building, how the economy was tied to it, the people who lived in it, the crafts, and the writing. Then explain in a sentence why the chapter calls Sumer the earliest city-based civilisation.
questions.a: Main building: the ziggurat for the chief god, around which the city grew, with palaces and royal storehouses nearby. Economy: agriculture, trade and transport of goods were tied to the temple authority. People: kings in palaces, people in small brick houses, priests and priestesses with restricted entry, merchants and traders. Crafts: metalworking, pottery and textiles. The chapter calls it the earliest city-based civilisation because the Sumerians were the first to evolve into one, at Ur and several other cities of Sumer.
s: Ziggurat and the city around it
Economy tied to the temple
People and hierarchy
Crafts
Writing and the closing sentence

questions.q:
Read the statements about the cities of Mesopotamia.
1. Cities that spoke different languages could not share a script, so each city kept its own writing.
2. Assur, in northern Mesopotamia, became the city-state that supplanted the Akkadian empire around 2154 BCE.

questions.q:
Match each Mesopotamian civilisation with what the chapter says about it.
1. Sumerians
2. Akkadians
3. Assyrians
4. Babylonians
a. Supplanted the Akkadians from Assur, in the north

questions.q:
A merchant of Akkad can load 12 shiploads for either of two eastern ports. Port P (Meluhha) gives goods worth 70 units a load but the round trip takes 50 days. Port Q (Dilmun) gives goods worth 40 units a load and takes 20 days. The goods at P include ivory, timber, gold dust and beads; Q has fewer of these.
(a) Which present-day region does the chapter identify with Meluhha, and which with Dilmun?
(b) Compute the value of a full cargo at each port and the value earned per day of travel.
(c) The merchant will repeat whichever route she picks as often as the season allows. Which should she choose? Use your figures and say what she gives up.
questions.a: (a) Meluhha is generally identified with the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation; Dilmun is today's Bahrain. (b) P: 12 times 70 is 840 units, which is 16.8 a day; Q: 12 times 40 is 480 units, which is 24 a day. (c) Either choice. Q earns more per day; P gives a larger cargo with ivory, timber, gold dust and beads, but earns less per day and ties up the ship for 50 days.
s: (a) Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation and Bahrain
(b) 840 and 480 units, 16.8 and 24 a day
(c) A choice with what is given up

questions.q: Maya says, 'Mesopotamian traders got semiprecious stone beads, ivory, timber, gold dust and copper from the Harappans.' Test her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Mostly right. The chapter says that with the Harappans, the Mesopotamians traded semiprecious stone beads, ivory, timber and gold dust, and probably copper. The word 'probably' means copper is not certain, so Maya should not state it as a fact.
s: Verdict: right except for one item
Beads, ivory, timber and gold dust match the chapter
Copper is only 'probably' traded

questions.q: A clock-maker copies the Sumerian base-60 idea: 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour. How many seconds are there in a 3-hour school examination?
questions.a: 10,800 seconds. 3 hours is 3 times 60 minutes, which is 180 minutes, and 180 times 60 seconds is 10,800 seconds. The chapter credits the Sumerians with the 60-minute hour and 60-second minute.
o: 10,800 seconds
1,800 seconds
3,600 seconds
108,000 seconds

questions.q: (a) The Akkadians took power in 2334 BCE and lost supremacy around 2154 BCE. How long did their dominance last? (b) Taking 1700 BCE, the Assyrians lasted from 2154 BCE to 1700 BCE; for how many years was that, and how many more than the Akkadian years in (a)?
questions.a: (a) 2334 minus 2154 is 180 years. (b) 2154 minus 1700 is 454 years, which is 274 years more than 180 years.
s: (a) 180 years
(b) 454 years, 274 years more

questions.q:
Imagine a governor of Babylon around 1450 BCE who has a budget of 600 units. New weapons for the army cost 400 units, and restoring exhausted farmland costs 350 units. He can do only what the budget allows.
(a) Which of the chapter's reasons for Babylon's decline does each spending choice answer?
(b) By how much would the cost of both exceed his budget?
(c) Choose one for this year, and say which reason from the chapter you leave unanswered and what could follow.
questions.a: (a) Weapons answer the attacks by the Hittites, who had mastered new technologies; farmland restoration answers environmental degradation and pressure on agricultural lands. (b) 400 plus 350 is 750 units, which is 150 units over 600. (c) Either choice, with the unanswered reason named. For example, choosing weapons leaves the farmland problem, which can keep weakening production.
s: (a) Each choice matched to a reason from the chapter
(b) 750 units, 150 over
(c) A choice with the unanswered reason and a consequence

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Cuneiform scribes in Mesopotamia enjoyed a high status in society, similar to the priests and priestesses.
Reason (R): Cuneiform was written by pressing a wedge-shaped stylus into soft clay tablets.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both statements are in the chapter, but the way cuneiform was written does not explain why scribes were highly regarded.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: Write a short note a Sumerian scribe might press into a clay tablet at a temple, using three details from the chapter, and say what a historian can learn from it.
questions.a: Example: 'Twelve potters delivered pots to the ziggurat; the priests have recorded the amount.' Three chapter details

questions.q: A student reads that traders from Sargon's Akkad carried semiprecious stone beads, ivory, timber and gold dust from lands in the east. Which statement matches the chapter?
questions.a: Meluhha is generally identified with the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, and Dilmun and Magan with Bahrain and Oman. The chapter says Sargon's cuneiform tablets talk about trade with the eastern territories of Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha; Meluhha is generally identified with the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, and Dilmun and Magan are today's Bahrain and the Oman peninsula.

Meluhha is identified with Babylon, and Dilmun and Magan with Assur and its neighbouring cities

questions.q: Explain three reasons why the Babylonians lost their earlier prominence by the end of 1400 BCE.
questions.a: Repeated attacks by the Hittites and other rising powers, who had mastered new technologies and more efficient ways of using natural resources; environmental degradation and pressure on agricultural lands; and internal political and economic problems. Together these weakened Babylonian control.
s: External pressure from the Hittites with their technology
Environmental degradation and pressure on agricultural lands
Internal political and economic problems

questions.q: (a) Name three kinds of writing that the cuneiform tablets have preserved besides records of work. (b) Which kind of tablet would tell a historian most about how the economy ran, and what did it list?
questions.a: (a) Any three of: myths and epics, hymns, law codes, educational treatises. (b) The tablets that kept a record of farming and craft activities, especially of potters, seal cutters, shipbuilders, carpenters and farm workers.
s: (a) Three kinds of writing from the list
(b) Records of farming and craft activities, with the workers named

questions.q: The Sumerians began writing around 3200 BCE and Hammurabi's rise is dated to 1792 BCE, which is ___ years later.
Explain how farming, copper and canals together helped Sumerian cities to emerge in Mesopotamia. Use the dates and details the chapter gives.
questions.a: Farming began in the region about 12,000 years before the present, in the fertile crescent's fertile land. Copper tools arrived around 4500 BCE and improved agriculture, craft production and trade, and helped farming spread across the plains of the Euphrates and Tigris. The Sumerians built dams and canals for irrigation and used mud bricks and burnt bricks. Surplus from farming supported craftsmen, merchants and priests, and large cities such as Ur grew and became city-states. The chapter says all of this led to the earliest city-based civilisation.

Copper tools and their effect with the date
Dams, canals and bricks

A conclusion linking these to the first cities

questions.a: The Hittites gave up their new technologies and stopped attacking. The chapter names attacks by the Hittites who mastered new technologies, environmental degradation, pressure on agricultural lands and internal political and economic problems.
o: The Hittites gave up their new technologies and stopped attacking
Repeated attacks by the Hittites and other rising powers
