questions.q: Differentiate the Sumerians from the Akkadians by language, script and what each is remembered for in the chapter.
questions.a: The Sumerians spoke Sumerian and were the earliest to evolve into a city-based civilisation, starting cuneiform. The Akkadians spoke Akkadian, a different language, but used the same cuneiform script; they established the world's first dynastic empire.
s: Language and script compared
What each is remembered for

questions.q: Cleopatra lived from 69 to 30 BCE and became queen at eighteen. Show that she could not have celebrated a Sed festival for her own 30th year on the throne, and name the festival's meaning.
questions.a: She became queen in 69 minus 18, which is 51 BCE. Her 30th year on the throne would be 51 minus 30, which is 21 BCE, which is 9 years after her death in 30 BCE. The Sed festival marked a king's 30th year on the throne, so she could not have celebrated it.
s: Year she became queen: 51 BCE
30th year would be 21 BCE, after her death in 30 BCE
Meaning of the Sed festival

questions.q: A student asks why the black stone found in 1799 was such a breakthrough for reading the Egyptian script. Which answer follows the chapter?
questions.a: It carried writing of three types, including Greek, which people could still read. The chapter says the Rosetta Stone had three types of writing, including Greek. Since people could still read Greek, it was like a bilingual dictionary for a lost language, and Champollion deciphered the script in 1822.
o: It carried writing of three types, including Greek, which people could still read
It carried only Greek writing, which Champollion translated in the same year of 1799
It was a list of pharaohs written in cuneiform by Sumerian scribes on soft clay

s: Verdict: False
Reason from the chapter, with the corrected statement

questions.q: Explain why the Egyptians built pyramids and how the pyramid form developed. Include the burial practice, the belief behind it, the preservation of the body, and one named example.
questions.a: Pharaohs were buried deep underground with a rectangular mastaba placed over the burial chamber. Gradually mastabas were placed one on top of the other to form a pyramid, such as the step pyramid at Saqqara. The Egyptians believed each person had a ka, a spiritual double, that lived on after death if the body was preserved through mummification, which removed the internal organs except the heart, dried the body with natron, oiled it, wrapped it in linen and placed it in a coffin.
s: Burial deep underground with a mastaba
Mastabas stacked to form a pyramid

Mummification as the way of preserving the body

questions.q: A visitor to Saqqara asks why Egyptians built such huge pyramids over their rulers' graves. What reason does the chapter give?
questions.a: They believed each person had a ka that lived on after death if the body was preserved. The chapter says pyramids were built primarily because the Egyptians believed each person had a ka, a spiritual double, that lived on after death if the body was preserved through mummification.
o: They believed each person had a ka that lived on after death if the body was preserved
They wanted to store the Nile's flood water in the pyramids for the dry months of the year
They needed a high tower from which to watch for the rising of Sirius each year
They copied the stepped temples called ziggurats from the cities of Sumer far away

questions.q: (a) What did Pierre Bouchard find in 1799, and who deciphered its script in 1822? (b) How many years passed between the find and the decipherment, and what made the find so useful?
questions.a: (a) The Rosetta Stone, a giant black stone covered with writing; Jean-Francois Champollion deciphered it. (b) 1822 minus 1799 is 23 years; it carried three types of writing including Greek, which could still be read, like a bilingual dictionary for a lost language.
s: (a) Rosetta Stone and Champollion
(b) 23 years, with Greek as the key

questions.q:
Read the statements about early Egypt.
1. The Nile flooded every winter, leaving rich mud which the Egyptians called kemet.
2. Mastabas were placed one on top of the other to form a pyramid, as in the step pyramid at Saqqara.
3. The Sed festival was held to mark a king's 30th year on the throne.

questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: the Nile flooded every summer. Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter.

questions.q: Name the three Egyptian seasons, with the time of year and activity the chapter gives for each.
questions.a: Inundation (autumn), when the Nile flooded; Peret (winter), the growing season; Shemu (summer), the harvest season. Each has four months.

Time of year and activity for each

questions.q:
A priest-scribe finds that his 365-day calendar, based on the rising of Sirius, has lost time since the real year is about a quarter of a day longer. A colleague suggests adding one extra day every fourth year. The treasurer notes that each extra festival day costs the temple 8,000 units of grain, and that the planting month will otherwise drift by one 30-day month in 120 years.
(a) How is the 365-day year built from months, and what does the lost time come to each year?
(b) How many days will the calendar have drifted in 60 years, and how many extra days would the colleague's fix add over the same 60 years?
(c) Should the temple adopt the fix? Weigh the cost against the drift, and say what the temple risks if it does nothing.
questions.a: (a) 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days; a quarter of a day is lost each year. (b) In 60 years the drift is 60 times 0.25, which is 15 days; one extra day every fourth year adds 60 divided by 4, which is 15 days, at 15 times 8,000, which is 120,000 units of grain. (c) Either choice. The fix keeps the seasons aligned with the months; doing nothing saves grain but the calendar drifts against inundation, peret and shemu.
s: (a) 12 times 30 plus 5, and a quarter of a day lost each year
(b) 15 days of drift and 15 extra days costing 120,000 units
(c) A choice with the risk or cost weighed

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The need to dig ditches and build dams in early Egypt is linked to the probable growth of local government.

questions.q: Which statement about the lives of women in early Egypt is NOT supported by the chapter?

questions.q: Explain three ways in which the Nile's yearly flood shaped life and organisation in early Egypt.
questions.a: The flood left rich mud, kemet, which was excellent for growing crops. Counting the days between floods helped the Egyptians develop a calendar. Digging ditches and building dams to use the flood water needed collective effort, which probably led to local government and an administrative class.

Calendar from counting days between floods
Collective effort and local government

questions.q: Put the stages of mummification in the order the chapter gives them, naming at least four.

s: Organs removed except the heart, then drying with natron
Oiling, wrapping, coffin and burial in order

questions.q: List five different sources the chapter names for what we know about Egypt, and say what each tells us or how it was used. Then say which of the five is closest to the Egyptians' own words and why.
questions.a: Greek writers such as Herodotus, who visited and wrote about Egypt in the 5th century BCE; the 19th century collection de L'Egypte; papyrus records, such as the Papyrus Ebers with more than 700 cures and spells; libraries from about 2000 BCE with scrolls in labelled jars, including early forms of Sindbad the Sailor and Cinderella; and the Rosetta Stone, whose script Champollion deciphered in 1822. s: Herodotus and de L'Egypte

Libraries with their scrolls

questions.q: The Egyptian calendar has 365 days, but the real year is about a quarter of a day longer. If nothing is adjusted, by about how many days will the calendar fall behind the seasons in 40 years?
questions.a: About 10 days. A quarter of a day each year over 40 years is 0.25 times 40, which is 10 days. The chapter says the calendar was quite accurate but lost time because the real year is about a quarter day longer.
o: About 10 days
About 4 days
About 40 days
About 100 days

questions.q: Farid says, 'The Egyptians named their land Kemet, meaning the black, after the colour of the soil that the Nile's flood left on the valley.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the river flooded every summer, leaving rich mud, called kemet, and that Egyptians referred to their land as Kemet, meaning 'the black', from the black river valley soil. His claim matches the chapter.
s: Verdict: the claim is right
The yearly flood left rich black mud
Kemet means 'the black', from the valley soil

questions.q: The Egyptian year has 12 months of 30 days. To make 365 days, ___ extra days are added.

Before a Nile flood, 60 villagers must dig 1,800 m of ditches. Each digs 6 m a day. The flood is due in 6 days. A village elder proposes making 4 villagers overseers, who plan the work and settle disputes but do not dig.
(a) Which feature of early Egypt does the elder's proposal begin to resemble, according to the chapter?
(b) How many days will the digging take with all 60 digging, and with 56 digging (round up to a whole day)?

With 56: 56 times 6 is 336 m a day, and 1,800 divided by 336 is about 5.36, so 6 days. (c) Either choice. With overseers the work just meets the 6-day limit with no margin; without them it finishes with a day to spare but the work may go less well organised.

questions.q: A goldsmith who owns his workshop and sells to merchants but holds no office is placed on the chapter's social hierarchy pyramid of early Egypt. Where does he belong?

questions.q: (a) By how many days does a 365-day calendar fall behind a year that is a quarter of a day longer, every year? (b) After how many years would this slippage add up to one whole 30-day Egyptian month?

(b) 120 years

questions.q: Explain three features that the major Bronze Age civilisations of the world shared, according to the chapter.
questions.a: They emerged independently in fertile river plains. Harnessing agricultural productivity and new resources helped economic growth and led to urban cities. They developed social and administrative systems, and writing systems to record economic transactions and social activities, which later led to literary and creative texts.

Agricultural productivity and urban cities
Administration and writing

questions.q: Under the Zhou, the people of a region have gone hungry for several harvests. What does the chapter say about the ruler's position?

o: He could be dismissed, since the chapter says rulers could be removed when their people did not prosper
